title: shortest paths
tags: Data structures and algorithms, in Python
statement:
Python Engineer · Data structures and algorithms, in Python

Build shortest_paths

Dijkstra: shortest distance from start to every reachable node.

>>> shortest_paths({"a": [("b", 4), ("c", 2)], "c": [("b", 1)], "b": []}, "a")

{'a': 0, 'c': 2, 'b': 3}

- Use heapq with the LAZY deletion trick: push (distance, node) and skip a popped

node you've already settled. Python's heap has no decrease-key.

- Unreachable nodes are absent from the result (not infinity).

- A negative weight raises ValueError — Dijkstra is simply wrong with those, and

silently returning a wrong answer is the worst possible behaviour.

- An unknown start raises KeyError.

Hint

Start with the smallest example in the contract. Read the named failing test; separate the normal behavior from validation and edge cases. Related helpers share this module workspace.

Module concepts & examples

22 — Data structures and algorithms, in Python

You did this in your degree. This module is about the *Python* layer on top: which

stdlib tool already implements the structure you were about to hand-roll, and how the

classic algorithms look when written idiomatically.

In plain English

Two things here: knowing which tools already exist, and knowing how to talk about cost.

The tools. Python ships with a priority queue (heapq), a double-ended queue

(deque), binary search (bisect), and a topological sort (graphlib). People reimplement

these constantly, usually worse. Writing them yourself once, to understand them, is a great

exercise — shipping your own version is usually a mistake.

The cost language. "Big-O" sounds academic but the idea is simple: *when the input gets

bigger, how much worse does this get?*

- O(1) — same cost no matter what. Looking up a word in a dictionary.

- O(log n) — barely grows. Guessing a number 1–1,000,000 by halving takes 20 guesses.

- O(n) — grows in step. Reading every page of a book.

- O(n log n) — the practical limit for sorting.

- O(n²) — grows *brutally*. Everyone shaking hands with everyone else.

The whole point is what happens as things scale. An O(n²) algorithm on 100 items is

instant. The same code on 100,000 items does ten billion operations and looks like it has

frozen. Same code, no bug — just the wrong shape.

Watch out for: Python's recursion limit (~1000 calls deep) and the lack of tail-call

optimisation. A recursion that's elegant in a textbook can simply crash here; the lesson

shows how to convert it to a loop.

1. Use the batteries first

You were about to writeUse instead
A dynamic arraylist
A hash map / setdict / set (open addressing, C-speed)
A doubly-linked list, queue, ring buffercollections.deque
A binary heap / priority queueheapq
A sorted-array insert or binary searchbisect
An LRU cachefunctools.lru_cache, or OrderedDict.move_to_end
A counter / multisetcollections.Counter
A grouping dictcollections.defaultdict
A merge of sorted streamsheapq.merge
A topological sortgraphlib.TopologicalSorter (3.9+)

Writing these yourself is a *learning* exercise (and this module makes you do a few). In

production code, the stdlib version is C, tested by millions of users, and shorter.

2. Complexity, with Python's constant factors

Big-O is necessary and not sufficient — an O(n log n) numpy sort beats an O(n) pure-Python

loop until n gets big, because the constant factor is ~50×.

StructureAccessSearchInsertDelete
listO(1)O(n)O(1) end, O(n) middleO(n)
dequeO(n)O(n)O(1) both endsO(1) both ends
dict/set—O(1) avgO(1) avgO(1) avg
heapqO(1) minO(n)O(log n)O(log n) pop-min
sorted list + bisectO(1)O(log n)O(n) (the shift)O(n)

Amortised analysis matters: list.append is O(1) *amortised* because the array doubles.

3. Recursion in Python

The recursion limit is ~1000 frames and there's no tail-call optimisation. So:

- Convert deep recursion to iteration with an explicit stack.

- Memoise with functools.cache — it turns exponential recursions into linear ones.

- sys.setrecursionlimit is a way to turn a clean RecursionError into a segfault; it's

not a fix.

- Divide and conquer on a balanced structure (depth ~log n) is fine recursively.

4. Sorting

sorted()/list.sort() are Timsort: O(n log n) worst case, O(n) on nearly-sorted

input, and stable. You will not beat it in Python.

What you actually need to know:

- key= is computed once per element (a Schwartzian transform, for free).

- Stability lets you sort by secondary key first, then primary.

- heapq.nlargest(k, it) is O(n log k) — better than sorting for small k.

- bisect.insort keeps a list sorted at O(n) per insert (the memmove is cheap; the

algorithmic cost is real).

Know *why* quicksort/mergesort/heapsort differ (in-place vs stable vs worst case) for the

interview; reach for sorted in the job.

5. Graphs

Represent as dict[node, list[node]] — an adjacency map. Then:

- BFS with a deque → shortest path in an unweighted graph.

- DFS with an explicit stack (or recursion when depth is bounded) → cycles,

components, topological order.

- Dijkstra with heapq → shortest path with non-negative weights. Use the lazy

variant: push (distance, node), and skip a popped node you've already settled.

- Topological sort → graphlib.TopologicalSorter, or Kahn's algorithm with in-degrees.

A cycle means "no valid order" — detect it, don't loop forever.

- A* is Dijkstra plus a heuristic; correct only when the heuristic never overestimates.

6. Dynamic programming

Two forms of the same thing:

- Top-down: plain recursion + @functools.cache. Write the recurrence, add one

decorator, done.

- Bottom-up: fill a table. More code, no recursion limit, and you can often drop to

O(width) memory by keeping only the last row.

The recurrence is the hard part; the code is mechanical.

7. Interview-shaped patterns worth having ready

Two pointers, sliding window (module 02's sliding_max), fast/slow pointers (cycle

detection), prefix sums, monotonic stack/deque, binary search on the answer, union-find,

backtracking with pruning, top-k with a heap.

8. Measure before you optimise

An O(n²) algorithm on n=100 is 10,000 operations — instant. Correct and simple beats

clever until the profiler (module 13) says otherwise.

Exercises

exercises_22.py, then pytest 22_algorithms. Several are deliberately "reimplement what

the stdlib gives you" — the tests check both correctness *and* complexity, so a working

but quadratic answer fails.

Further reading

- heapq (optional reading: https://docs.python.org/3/library/heapq.html), bisect (optional reading: https://docs.python.org/3/library/bisect.html), graphlib (optional reading: https://docs.python.org/3/library/graphlib.html)

- *Introduction to Algorithms* (CLRS) for the theory; LeetCode/Advent of Code for the reps

import random
import time

import pytest

from courselib import impl

m = impl("22")


def timed(fn) -> float:
    start = time.perf_counter()
    fn()
    return time.perf_counter() - start


class TestBinarySearch:
    def test_found(self):
        assert m.binary_search([1, 3, 5, 7], 5) == 2

    def test_first_and_last(self):
        assert m.binary_search([1, 3, 5, 7], 1) == 0
        assert m.binary_search([1, 3, 5, 7], 7) == 3

    def test_not_found(self):
        assert m.binary_search([1, 3, 5, 7], 4) == -1

    def test_empty(self):
        assert m.binary_search([], 1) == -1

    def test_single(self):
        assert m.binary_search([5], 5) == 0
        assert m.binary_search([5], 1) == -1

    def test_duplicates_return_a_valid_index(self):
        items = [1, 2, 2, 2, 3]
        assert items[m.binary_search(items, 2)] == 2

    def test_strings(self):
        assert m.binary_search(["a", "c", "e"], "c") == 1

    def test_matches_bruteforce(self):
        rng = random.Random(7)
        for _ in range(50):
            items = sorted(rng.sample(range(200), rng.randint(0, 40)))
            target = rng.randint(0, 200)
            got = m.binary_search(items, target)
            assert (got == -1) == (target not in items)
            if got != -1:
                assert items[got] == target

    @pytest.mark.benchmark
    def test_is_logarithmic(self):
        items = list(range(5_000_000))
        assert timed(lambda: [m.binary_search(items, n) for n in range(0, 5_000_000, 250_000)]) < 0.1


class TestMergeIntervals:
    def test_basic(self):
        assert m.merge_intervals([(1, 3), (2, 6), (8, 10), (15, 18)]) == [(1, 6), (8, 10), (15, 18)]

    def test_touching_merges(self):
        assert m.merge_intervals([(1, 4), (4, 5)]) == [(1, 5)]

    def test_unsorted_input(self):
        assert m.merge_intervals([(8, 10), (1, 3), (2, 6)]) == [(1, 6), (8, 10)]

    def test_contained_interval(self):
        assert m.merge_intervals([(1, 10), (3, 5)]) == [(1, 10)]

    def test_identical(self):
        assert m.merge_intervals([(1, 2), (1, 2)]) == [(1, 2)]

    def test_empty(self):
        assert m.merge_intervals([]) == []

    def test_single(self):
        assert m.merge_intervals([(1, 2)]) == [(1, 2)]

    def test_zero_width(self):
        assert m.merge_intervals([(1, 1), (2, 2)]) == [(1, 1), (2, 2)]

    def test_invalid_interval(self):
        with pytest.raises(ValueError):
            m.merge_intervals([(5, 1)])

    @pytest.mark.benchmark
    def test_is_n_log_n(self):
        rng = random.Random(1)
        intervals = [(s := rng.randint(0, 10**6), s + rng.randint(0, 100)) for _ in range(200_000)]
        assert timed(lambda: m.merge_intervals(intervals)) < 2.0


class TestLRUCache:
    def test_get_and_put(self):
        cache = m.LRUCache(2)
        cache.put("a", 1)
        assert cache.get("a") == 1

    def test_missing_returns_default(self):
        cache = m.LRUCache(2)
        assert cache.get("nope") is None
        assert cache.get("nope", "fallback") == "fallback"

    def test_evicts_least_recently_used(self):
        cache = m.LRUCache(2)
        cache.put("a", 1)
        cache.put("b", 2)
        cache.get("a")  # "a" is now the most recently used
        cache.put("c", 3)
        assert cache.get("b") is None
        assert cache.get("a") == 1

    def test_update_refreshes_recency(self):
        cache = m.LRUCache(2)
        cache.put("a", 1)
        cache.put("b", 2)
        cache.put("a", 10)
        cache.put("c", 3)
        assert cache.get("b") is None
        assert cache.get("a") == 10

    def test_capacity_one(self):
        cache = m.LRUCache(1)
        cache.put("a", 1)
        cache.put("b", 2)
        assert cache.get("a") is None and cache.get("b") == 2

    def test_len_and_contains(self):
        cache = m.LRUCache(2)
        cache.put("a", 1)
        assert len(cache) == 1
        assert "a" in cache
        assert "b" not in cache

    def test_contains_is_not_a_use(self):
        cache = m.LRUCache(2)
        cache.put("a", 1)
        cache.put("b", 2)
        assert "a" in cache  # must not refresh "a"
        cache.put("c", 3)
        assert "a" not in cache

    def test_counters(self):
        cache = m.LRUCache(1)
        cache.put("a", 1)
        cache.get("a")
        cache.get("missing")
        cache.put("b", 2)
        assert (cache.hits, cache.misses, cache.evictions) == (1, 1, 1)

    def test_clear(self):
        cache = m.LRUCache(2)
        cache.put("a", 1)
        cache.clear()
        assert len(cache) == 0

    def test_rejects_bad_capacity(self):
        with pytest.raises(ValueError):
            m.LRUCache(0)

    @pytest.mark.benchmark
    def test_operations_are_constant_time(self):
        cache = m.LRUCache(1000)

        def hammer():
            for n in range(200_000):
                cache.put(n, n)
                cache.get(n - 500)

        assert timed(hammer) < 2.0  # an O(n) eviction scan would take minutes


class TestTopologicalSort:
    def test_chain(self):
        assert m.topological_sort({"a": ["b"], "b": ["c"], "c": []}) == ["a", "b", "c"]

    def test_diamond(self):
        order = m.topological_sort({"a": ["b", "c"], "b": ["d"], "c": ["d"], "d": []})
        assert order.index("a") < order.index("b") < order.index("d")
        assert order.index("c") < order.index("d")

    def test_independent_nodes(self):
        assert sorted(m.topological_sort({"a": [], "b": []})) == ["a", "b"]

    def test_empty(self):
        assert m.topological_sort({}) == []

    def test_node_only_appearing_as_a_successor(self):
        assert m.topological_sort({"a": ["b"]}) == ["a", "b"]

    def test_cycle_raises(self):
        with pytest.raises(ValueError, match="cycle"):
            m.topological_sort({"a": ["b"], "b": ["a"]})

    def test_self_loop_raises(self):
        with pytest.raises(ValueError):
            m.topological_sort({"a": ["a"]})

    def test_partial_cycle_raises(self):
        with pytest.raises(ValueError):
            m.topological_sort({"a": ["b"], "b": ["c"], "c": ["b"]})

    def test_every_edge_is_respected(self):
        rng = random.Random(3)
        nodes = list(range(200))
        graph = {n: [] for n in nodes}
        for n in nodes:
            for target in rng.sample(nodes[n + 1 :], min(3, len(nodes) - n - 1)):
                graph[n].append(target)
        order = m.topological_sort(graph)
        position = {node: i for i, node in enumerate(order)}
        assert all(position[a] < position[b] for a, targets in graph.items() for b in targets)


class TestShortestPaths:
    GRAPH = {"a": [("b", 4), ("c", 2)], "b": [("d", 5)], "c": [("b", 1), ("d", 8)], "d": []}

    def test_distances(self):
        assert m.shortest_paths(self.GRAPH, "a") == {"a": 0, "b": 3, "c": 2, "d": 8}

    def test_prefers_the_cheaper_route(self):
        assert m.shortest_paths(self.GRAPH, "a")["b"] == 3  # a->c->b beats a->b

    def test_start_has_distance_zero(self):
        assert m.shortest_paths(self.GRAPH, "d") == {"d": 0}

    def test_unreachable_nodes_are_absent(self):
        graph = {"a": [], "b": [("a", 1)]}
        assert m.shortest_paths(graph, "a") == {"a": 0}

    def test_unknown_start(self):
        with pytest.raises(KeyError):
            m.shortest_paths(self.GRAPH, "zzz")

    def test_negative_weight_raises(self):
        with pytest.raises(ValueError):
            m.shortest_paths({"a": [("b", -1)], "b": []}, "a")

    def test_zero_weights(self):
        assert m.shortest_paths({"a": [("b", 0)], "b": []}, "a") == {"a": 0, "b": 0}

    @pytest.mark.benchmark
    def test_scales(self):
        # A 100k-node chain: fine with a heap, hopeless with a linear-scan minimum.
        graph = {n: [(n + 1, 1)] for n in range(100_000)}
        graph[100_000] = []
        assert timed(lambda: m.shortest_paths(graph, 0)) < 2.0


class TestEditDistance:
    @pytest.mark.parametrize(
        ("a", "b", "expected"),
        [
            ("kitten", "sitting", 3),
            ("flaw", "lawn", 2),
            ("", "abc", 3),
            ("abc", "", 3),
            ("", "", 0),
            ("same", "same", 0),
            ("a", "b", 1),
            ("abcdef", "abcdef", 0),
        ],
    )
    def test_cases(self, a, b, expected):
        assert m.edit_distance(a, b) == expected

    def test_symmetric(self):
        assert m.edit_distance("kitten", "sitting") == m.edit_distance("sitting", "kitten")

    @pytest.mark.benchmark
    def test_large_inputs(self):
        rng = random.Random(11)
        a = "".join(rng.choice("abcd") for _ in range(2000))
        b = "".join(rng.choice("abcd") for _ in range(2000))
        assert timed(lambda: m.edit_distance(a, b)) < 5.0


class TestLongestIncreasingSubsequence:
    @pytest.mark.parametrize(
        ("values", "expected"),
        [
            ([10, 9, 2, 5, 3, 7, 101, 18], 4),
            ([1, 2, 3, 4], 4),
            ([4, 3, 2, 1], 1),
            ([], 0),
            ([5], 1),
            ([2, 2, 2], 1),  # strictly increasing, so duplicates don't extend it
            ([1, 3, 2, 4], 3),
        ],
    )
    def test_cases(self, values, expected):
        assert m.longest_increasing_subsequence(values) == expected

    @pytest.mark.benchmark
    def test_is_n_log_n(self):
        rng = random.Random(5)
        values = [rng.randint(0, 10**9) for _ in range(100_000)]
        assert timed(lambda: m.longest_increasing_subsequence(values)) < 2.0

"""Module 22 exercises.  pytest 22_algorithms

The tests check complexity as well as correctness: several of them run inputs large
enough that a quadratic answer times out. Reach for `heapq`, `bisect`, `deque` and
`functools.cache` — and hand-roll only where the exercise says to.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from collections.abc import Hashable, Iterable, Sequence
from typing import Any, TypeVar

T = TypeVar("T")
Node = TypeVar("Node", bound=Hashable)


def binary_search(items: Sequence[Any], target: Any) -> int:
    """Return the index of `target` in a sorted sequence, or -1.

    >>> binary_search([1, 3, 5, 7], 5)
    2
    >>> binary_search([1, 3, 5, 7], 4)
    -1

    Write the loop yourself (this one IS the learning exercise), then note that
    `bisect.bisect_left` plus a bounds check is the production answer.

    Get the invariant right: `lo <= hi`, and `mid = lo + (hi - lo) // 2`. Duplicates may
    return any matching index.
    """
    raise NotImplementedError


def merge_intervals(intervals: Iterable[tuple[int, int]]) -> list[tuple[int, int]]:
    """Merge overlapping or touching intervals.

    >>> merge_intervals([(1, 3), (2, 6), (8, 10), (15, 18)])
    [(1, 6), (8, 10), (15, 18)]
    >>> merge_intervals([(1, 4), (4, 5)])
    [(1, 5)]

    - Input order is arbitrary; output is sorted by start.
    - Touching counts as overlapping ((1,4) and (4,5) merge).
    - An interval with start > end raises ValueError.
    - Empty input -> [].

    Sort once, then a single pass: O(n log n) total, no nested loop.
    """
    raise NotImplementedError


class LRUCache:
    """A fixed-capacity LRU cache with O(1) get and put.

    >>> cache = LRUCache(2)
    >>> cache.put("a", 1); cache.put("b", 2); cache.get("a")
    1
    >>> cache.put("c", 3)      # evicts "b", the least recently used
    >>> cache.get("b") is None
    True

    - `get(key, default=None)` returns the value and marks it most-recently-used.
    - `put(key, value)` inserts or updates, evicting the LRU entry when over capacity.
      Updating an existing key also refreshes it.
    - `len(cache)`, `key in cache` (which must NOT count as a use), `.clear()`.
    - `.hits` and `.misses` counters, and `.evictions`.
    - capacity < 1 raises ValueError.

    `collections.OrderedDict.move_to_end` and `popitem(last=False)` give you O(1). A list
    scan for the LRU entry is O(n) and the tests will catch it.
    """

    def __init__(self, capacity: int) -> None:
        raise NotImplementedError


def topological_sort(graph: dict[Node, list[Node]]) -> list[Node]:
    """Return an order where every node precedes its dependents. Raise ValueError on a cycle.

    `graph[node]` lists the nodes that `node` points TO (its successors).

    >>> topological_sort({"a": ["b"], "b": ["c"], "c": []})
    ['a', 'b', 'c']

    - Implement Kahn's algorithm: compute in-degrees, seed a queue with the zero-degree
      nodes, and peel. Do NOT just call `graphlib` — you're writing it once so you know
      what it does.
    - Ties are broken by insertion order of the graph dict, so the result is deterministic.
    - A node that only appears as a successor is still part of the graph.
    - A cycle raises ValueError listing the nodes still unprocessed.
    """
    raise NotImplementedError


def shortest_paths(
    graph: dict[Node, list[tuple[Node, float]]], start: Node
) -> dict[Node, float]:
    """Dijkstra: shortest distance from `start` to every reachable node.

    >>> shortest_paths({"a": [("b", 4), ("c", 2)], "c": [("b", 1)], "b": []}, "a")
    {'a': 0, 'c': 2, 'b': 3}

    - Use `heapq` with the LAZY deletion trick: push `(distance, node)` and skip a popped
      node you've already settled. Python's heap has no decrease-key.
    - Unreachable nodes are absent from the result (not infinity).
    - A negative weight raises ValueError — Dijkstra is simply wrong with those, and
      silently returning a wrong answer is the worst possible behaviour.
    - An unknown `start` raises KeyError.
    """
    raise NotImplementedError


def edit_distance(a: str, b: str) -> int:
    """Levenshtein distance: the fewest insert/delete/substitute edits from `a` to `b`.

    >>> edit_distance("kitten", "sitting")
    3

    Use the BOTTOM-UP form with only two rows of memory. The tests compare 2,000-character
    strings, so a naive recursion (exponential) or a full n*m table (400 MB) both fail.
    """
    raise NotImplementedError


def longest_increasing_subsequence(values: Sequence[int]) -> int:
    """Length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence (not substring).

    >>> longest_increasing_subsequence([10, 9, 2, 5, 3, 7, 101, 18])
    4

    The O(n^2) DP is the obvious answer; the tests use 100,000 elements, so you need the
    O(n log n) one: keep a list of the smallest possible tail for each length and place
    each value with `bisect_left`. That list is NOT the subsequence itself — only its
    length is meaningful.
    """
    raise NotImplementedError
